newsitem.title: USA: Nippon pondering appeal on criminal indictment.
newsitem.headline: Nippon pondering appeal on criminal indictment.

text.p: Nippon Paper Industries Inc. said Friday it was deciding whether to appeal a decision granting U.S. courts authority over alleged criminal antitrust conduct that took place in Japan.
Richard Parker, lead attorney for Nippon, said no decision had yet been made.

The First Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston expanded the reach of the Sherman antitrust act this week, holding that American authorities can pursue Nippon Paper Industries for a conspiracy to raise fax paper prices, even though the alleged conspiracy was in Japan.

Acting Assistant Attorney General Joel Klein said the decision grants his department power to protect U.S. consumers from international cartels. Klein, who has made international enforcement of antitrust laws one of his focuses, was gratified.
"This case is very important to the antitrust division's enforcement effort against international cartels that harm U.S. consumers," he said in a statement.
"We need to be able to reach such cartels no matter where the cartel activity takes place," he said.
But the decision may not be the last word. Parker said Nippon has 14 days to appeal the decision to the full circuit court -- instead of merely a panel -- or 90 days to appeal to the Supreme Court.

If there is no appeal, a criminal antitrust trial may go ahead. The court reinstated an indictment against Nippon, thrown out by a lower court, for conspiring to raise the price of thermal fax paper in North America.
"Section One of Sherman Act applies to wholly foreign conduct which has an intended and substantial effect in the United States," said the circuit court.

Nippon manufactures thermal facsimile paper. The indictment alleges Nippon and co-conspirators agreed to fix the prices of thermal fax paper in North America and monitored to make certain the prices charged to end users were those it arranged.

Nippon argued that any actions it may have taken were entirely in Japan and that it was unprecedented when "one nation seeks to apply its criminal laws to actions taken in a foreign country by nationals of that country."
The appeals court said that the alleged actions were illegal under both Japanese and U.S. law.
The court called this "an age of international commerce, where decisions reached in one corner of the world can reverberate around the globe in less time than it takes to tell the tale."
